items.text: The label (Vasostrict) indicates vasopressin to increase blood pressure in adults with vasodilatory shock who remain hypotensive despite fluids and catecholamines.

Vasopressin is an adjunct rather than the usual initial agent in adult septic shock; SSC 2026 conditionally favors adding it when norepinephrine requirements rise. A better arterial pressure does not rule out reduced cardiac output or regional ischemia.
Monitor serum electrolytes, fluid status and urine output after the drug is discontinued, as the label advises.
Haemodynamic monitoring frequency follows the unit's vasoactive infusion protocol.
After vasopressin is stopped, the label calls for monitoring of serum electrolytes, fluid status and urine output because reversible diabetes insipidus can occur.

Catecholamines can have additive pressor effects with vasopressin. Indomethacin may prolong its effect, and medicines that disturb water balance may change the pressor response. Review the medication history and communicate unexpected pressure or fluid-balance changes.
A decrease in cardiac index may be seen with vasopressin; the label warns it can worsen cardiac function.

Reversible diabetes insipidus (polyuria, pale watery urine and hypernatraemia) can follow cessation of treatment; some patients need the drug restarted or desmopressin, which are prescriber decisions.
The registered product lists ischaemic complications affecting the heart, bowel, skin and extremities, as well as low serum sodium and rhythm disturbances.

Vasostrict formulations differ in excipients. Known vasopressin hypersensitivity precludes use; the multidose product also carries a chlorobutanol hypersensitivity contraindication. Verify the exact presentation and allergy history with pharmacy.
The label notes that adverse reactions were identified from the literature and reported voluntarily, so their frequency cannot be estimated reliably.

The most common adverse reactions include decreased cardiac output, bradycardia, tachyarrhythmias, hyponatraemia and ischaemia (coronary, mesenteric, skin and digital); the label also lists right heart failure, atrial fibrillation, mesenteric ischaemia, acute renal insufficiency and reversible diabetes insipidus.
Escalate for worsening perfusion or cardiac function, a marked rise in urine output with a rising sodium after stopping, or any new arrhythmia.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record haemodynamics, urine output, electrolyte results and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Monitor haemodynamics at the unit's frequency.
After the drug is stopped, monitor urine output, fluid status and serum electrolytes.
Review serum sodium and other electrolyte results as ordered.
Report signs of worsening cardiac function or a sudden polyuria with pale watery urine.
Record urine output and electrolyte trends.
Assess for new peripheral colour or temperature changes, abdominal or cardiac concerns and deteriorating perfusion; review sodium trends and obtain urgent clinical assessment for suspected ischaemia.
After discontinuation, urgently report abrupt excessive watery urine, rising sodium or worsening fluid balance; monitor under the prescribed plan.
Confirm product presentation, excipient allergy and concurrent vasoactive medicines; escalate unexpected pressure, perfusion or fluid-balance changes.
